panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: A chest radiograph showing diffuse reticular nodular shadowing in a patient with clinical suspicion and biopsy results confirming iron granule deposition consistent with inert metal pneumoconiosis (siderosis). B: A CT scan showing bilateral tiny nodular opacities, predominantly in the mid and upper zones, in a patient with clinical and pathological findings consistent with inert metal pneumoconiosis.

plate_findings.evidence: Larger sized qualified nodules in the right upper lobe

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Panel A shows diffuse micronodular changes consistent with the diagnosis of inert metal pneumoconiosis as described in the caption and supported by the HRCT pattern. B: Panel B illustrates the presence of larger qualified nodules in the RUL and scattered dense nodules in the lower lobes, consistent with the HRCT description of pneumoconiosis. C: Panel C shows specific large nodular opacities located in the paraspinal cortex of the right lower lobe, supporting the diagnosis of inert metal pneumoconiosis.
panels.attribution_text: Delgado-García et al. Workers with Suspected Diagnosis of Silicosis: A Case Study of Sarcoidosis Versus Siderosis.. Healthcare (Basel, Switzerland) 2023. doi:10.3390/healthcare11121782. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 6.
panels.figure_caption: (A) Diffuse, segmentally distributed micronodular disease more predominant in the middle thirds. (B,C) Larger sized qualified nodules in the right upper lobe, other dense and irregular nodules in both lower lobes, with the most significant in the paraspinal cortex of the apical segment of the right lower lobe of 9 mm.
in_text_mentions: ckening of the bronchovascular axes, as well as an irregularity of the subpleural connective tissue; larger qualified nodules were located in the right upper lobe and other dense and irregular nodules in both lower lobes. The most significant one was in the paraspinal cortex of the apical segment of the right lower lobe, measuring 9 mm, with hilar thickening by discreetly enlarged ganglia. In the mediastinum, there were a few nodes smaller than 1 cm. These findings did not allow a diagnostic distinction to be made between pneumoconiosis and the possibility of an associated neoplasm (Figure 6).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: CT image (lung window) showing ground glass changes and multiple nodular foci, consistent with pneumoconiosis given the occupational history of the patient. B: CT image (mediastinal window) demonstrating a thick-walled cavity and peripheral nodular foci consistent with inert metal pneumoconiosis.
panels.attribution_text: Zhou et al. Case report: Application of morphology in the diagnosis of siderosis in a patient with tuberculosis infection.. Frontiers in oncology 2023. doi:10.3389/fonc.2023.1001802. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: (A) Lung window on chest CT. The figure shows the multiple “ground glass” blurred shadows on both lungs (shown by the white arrow); the upper lobe of the right lung shows multiple nodular foci, one of which is larger (shown by the black arrow), showing a thick-walled cavity, and the edge of the lesion has multiple small nodule foci (shown by the red arrow). (B) Mediastinal window on chest CT. The figure shows a thick-walled cavity shadow (shown by a black arrow) in a larger nodular foci of the upper lobe of the right lung. The inner wall of the cavity is still smooth, the adjacent pleural traction is changed, the marginal small nodule foci are slightly displayed (shown by the red arrow), and the deposition of granular materials is visible.

panels.rationale: The image is an axial orbital CT showing a hyperdense foreign body in the vitreous base. The article context links this metallic foreign body to the diagnosis of ocular siderosis (siderosis bulbi), which is strongly associated with metal dust exposure characteristic of inert metal pneumoconiosis.
panels.attribution_text: Chai et al. The Rusty Eye: Ocular Siderosis Masquerading as Chronic Anterior Uveitis.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.101280. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Axial view of the orbital computed tomography showing the presence of an intraocular foreign body (red arrow) located at the vitreous base.
in_text_mentions: In light of the history of the high-velocity metallic injury and the eye findings, siderosis bulbi was highly suspected. Computed tomography of the orbit showed the presence of a well-defined, hyperdense foreign body, which produced streak artifacts near the vitreous base (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: The CT scan displays fibronodular changes and diffuse centrilobular nodules in a patient whose clinical context and occupation strongly suggest pulmonary siderosis, a form of inert metal pneumoconiosis. Findings are supported by the caption and in-text mentions.

in_text_mentions: To further evaluate the respiratory compromise, a CT scan of the thorax was done, which showed diffuse centrilobular nodules in bilateral lungs and fibronodular changes in apical segments of both lungs, with centrilobular emphysema and subpleural hyperdense consolidation, suggestive of interstitial lung disease - most likely pulmonary siderosis in view of his occupation (Figures 2, 3).
